notes:
I've written notes on all 28 verses below, but some of what you asked for is missing. My search and page-reading limits ran out early. Guzik's Enduring Word page only loaded up to v. 12, and the full Pulpit Commentary page wouldn't open. I found nothing from the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran-site, Pentecostal-site or prosperity/hyper-grace sources, so those sections are left out, as you asked. Where I name a commentator's tradition (Gill as Baptist and so on), that label is my own, not something the pages say.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional:** Guzik says this baseless fear belongs to the wicked, "both because they are under God's displeasure and because they lack the strength and courage of the Holy Spirit." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- The righteous are bold because they have a clean conscience. They "don't always have to look over their shoulders", and their courage comes from God, not themselves. (Kingcomments) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html
- Matthew Henry (Concise): "Sin makes men cowards." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/28-2.htm
- **NET note:** the righteous have no need to look out for avengers or police, so they stand firm instead of running. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki

**v. 2**
- **Traditional:** Guzik reads "many rulers" as a curse, a bloated government sent because of a nation's sin. A wise leader, by contrast, is a blessing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** when evil abounds, a country "becomes the prey of pretenders and partisans striving for the supremacy", as the history of the northern kingdom of Israel shows. Benson's notes list Asa, Hezekiah and Josiah as wise kings who held off judgment for a time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/28-2.htm
- **Ironside:** "transgression" here means rebellion against lawful authority, which leads to rival leaders and lawless confusion. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/proverbs-28.html
- **Pulpit (Homiletics):** rebellion is justified only when there is very great wrong and a clear chance of success. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-28.html
- **Modern/textual (NET):** the many rulers may come at once or in quick succession, as in the time of the judges. The Greek Old Testament (LXX) has a different verse altogether, and the last line ("maintains order") is hard to translate. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki

**v. 3**
- **Traditional:** Guzik notes that the poor don't always sympathise with the poor. He cites Clarke's link to Jesus' parable of the unforgiving servant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- **Matthew Henry:** people who know poverty should be kind to others in it, and needy people who gain power are often especially grasping. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_028.cfm
- **Kingcomments:** a poor man raised to power could have been "refreshing rain" to his old peers, which makes his oppression tragic. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html
- **Modern/textual (NET):** the Hebrew reads "a poor man." Because the poor in Proverbs have no power to oppress, many scholars change one letter to get "a wicked ruler," though "There is no textual support for this change." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki
- The image is rain that ought to grow crops but doesn't. "a show of strength may not produce anything except ruin." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php/f/f/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&mode=print

**v. 4**
- **Traditional:** Guzik links "resisting" the wicked to Romans 13, where government exists partly to restrain evil. He quotes Kidner: once God's revealed law is dropped, morality becomes relative and nothing seems worth opposing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- **Ironside:** a man always ready to excuse wrong in others usually reveals his own uneasy conscience. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/proverbs-28.html
- **Kingcomments:** in a society that praises the wicked, God's Word has been thrown overboard. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html
- **Modern (NET):** the verb means "to engage in strife." The Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) adds "so as to induce them to repent." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki

**v. 5**
- **Traditional:** Poole says evil men's minds are blinded by their passions and by "the god of this world." Those who seek the Lord through his Word and prayer understand everything they need for their duty and their salvation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/28-5.htm
- Matthew Henry: seeking the Lord is both a sign of understanding and a way to gain more. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_028.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary links "understand all things" to 1 John 2:20 and John 7:17. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/28-5.htm
- **Modern (NET):** *mishpat* ("justice") means people's legal rights and fair decisions in the community. Plaut observes some people think justice is only whatever benefits them. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki

**v. 6**
- **Traditional:** Guzik says we are defined by our character, not our bank account. He quotes Ross that there are also honest rich people and crooked poor people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- Kingcomments reads "perverse" as hypocrisy: religious on the outside, greedy inside. It adds that wealth is not automatically proof of God's approval. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html
- **Modern (NET):** "ways" is a dual form in Hebrew ("two ways"), which suggests a hypocrite. NET rejects Toy's attempt to change the word. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki

**v. 7**
- **Traditional:** obedience proves wisdom, and merely keeping company with gluttons can shame a family. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- Matthew Henry: keeping God's law makes a son wise towards his parents too, because the law teaches him how to treat them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_028.cfm

**v. 8**
- **Traditional:** Barnes says ill-gotten gain does not last but passes to people who use it better. Poole and Gill read this as usury that oppresses the poor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/28-8.htm
- Matthew Henry: Providence sometimes moves unjust gain into charitable hands. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_028.cfm
- Guzik cites Waltke that such interest in Bible times ran at about 30%. Kidner notes the Law treated interest differently in business and in family care (Deut 23:19–20). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- **Modern (NET):** the two words for interest probably form one idea, "exorbitant interest." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki

**v. 9**
- **Traditional:** Guzik says we must listen to God's Word before we speak to him in prayer. He quotes Clarke that choosing not to know your duty does not excuse you. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- Pulpit (Homiletics): God does not hear every prayer. A penitent's broken words may be accepted while polished prayers are rejected. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-28.html

**v. 10**
- **Traditional:** the wicked are caught in their own schemes. Guzik notes Kidner's link to Jesus' warnings against causing others to stumble (Matt 18:6). He also quotes Ross that this shows the righteous *can* be led astray. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- Kingcomments applies the verse to modern pressure through advertising, the internet and the downplaying of adultery. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html

**v. 11**
- **Traditional:** the rich often credit their own cleverness for their success, but a discerning poor man sees through the show. Bridges points out that Christ himself chose poverty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- **Modern (NET):** the rich man "thinks he is wise because he is rich, that he has made all the right choices." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki

**v. 12**
- **Traditional:** Guzik quotes Trapp's examples of people forced into hiding: Moses, David, Elijah, and the infant Jesus fleeing Herod. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- Matthew Henry: there is "great glory" when the righteous have freedom to practise their faith and hold office. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_028.cfm
- Ironside: under evil rulers, even trustworthy men hide so as not to become targets. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/proverbs-28.html
- **Other readings:** the Pulpit Commentary mentions two others. Evil times test people's character. Or under wicked rulers, good men withdraw from public life. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-28.html
- Toy suggests the translation "great confidence" instead of "great glory." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki

**v. 13** (the verse where traditions most clearly differ)
- **Shared reading:** John MacArthur says the verse joins the two inseparable parts of true repentance, confessing sin and forsaking it. Bridges: the contrast is not between big and small sins but between hidden and confessed ones. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_2813_commentary
- **NET:** "covering" means refusing to admit sin and perhaps explaining it away. The verse is "unique in the book of Proverbs; it captures the theology of forgiveness". https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&verse=13
- **Gill (Baptist):** confess to other people where the offence calls for it, "but not to a priest, in order for absolution, which no man can give". He adds that confessing and forsaking do not earn pardon; mercy is not merit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/28-13.htm
- **Benson/Poole:** hiding sin is enough to condemn a man, but confession without forsaking is not enough to save him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/28-13.htm
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** the penitent is fully forgiven at once but may still bear earthly consequences, as David did (2 Sam 12:14). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/28-13.htm
- **Lutheran link (Keil & Delitzsch):** Luther's translation of this verse "lives in the mouth of the Christian people." Forgiveness does not follow confession unless it comes with *nova obedientia* (new obedience). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/28-13.htm
- One sermon on Precept Austin says confession is "the effect of divine mercy", not its cause. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_2813_commentary
- **Textual:** the Septuagint (Brenton) has a different second line: "he that blames himself shall be loved." https://biblehub.com/proverbs/28-13.htm

**v. 14**
- **Traditional (Kingcomments):** the "fear" here is mainly fear of sin rather than fear of the Lord, and a deep sense of sin is a special grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html
- **NET:** the hard-hearted person refuses to fear sin and its results, and so falls into sin. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php/f/f/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&mode=print

**v. 15**
- **Traditional:** a foolish tyrant over the poor is like a roaring lion or charging bear, unpredictable and destructive. (Guzik's summary of vv. 15–16) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- **Dispensational reading (Kingcomments):** sees the wicked ruler as a picture of the antichrist after the rapture, persecuting a believing remnant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html

**v. 16**
- **Traditional:** a wise, humble leader who hates greed blesses a nation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- Matthew Henry calls tyrants the greatest fools, because they give up their subjects' goodwill for absolute power. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_028.cfm
- **Scholarly:** Ewald, Delitzsch and others read the verse as a warning addressed to the ruler. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-28.html
- NET notes the LXX reads "lacks income" instead of "lacks understanding." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki

**v. 17**
- **Pulpit Homiletics (on this verse, it seems):** no pity is shown to the one who showed none. It calls this "no argument for capital punishment, but it is an argument for such a treatment of criminals as will best deter from crime." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/28.htm

**v. 18**
- **Traditional:** Pulpit Homiletics: "Integrity is alone safe"; sooner or later the sinner falls in his crooked ways. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/28.htm
- Kingcomments: the crooked man leaves God out of account, so no one delivers him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html
- **Ironside (on the walk of integrity, apparently v. 18):** the verse is not about saving the soul, since no one is justified by walking uprightly. It is about daily living in grace. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/proverbs-28.html

**v. 19**
- **NET:** "Prosperity depends on diligent work and not on chasing empty dreams." The same verb ("be filled") appears in both lines, with an ironic twist: filled with poverty. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki
- Kingcomments: the dreamer lives off other people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html

**v. 20**
- **Ironside:** the faithful man probably won't pile up great wealth but will be rich in heavenly treasure. The one whose life goal is riches will be called to account. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/proverbs-28.html
- Kingcomments: haste to get rich implies dishonest methods. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html

**v. 21**
- **NET:** "not good" is a deliberate understatement meaning "it is terrible!" https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki
- Kingcomments: a judge who shows favouritism is already corrupt, so a mere bribe of bread can sway him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html

**v. 22**
- **NET:** the Hebrew is "a man with an evil eye," the opposite of the generous "good eye": selfish and looking only to his own gain. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki
- Kingcomments: God will punish such greed with want. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html

**v. 23**
- Kingcomments: flatterers want something for themselves. Those who want to please God rebuke, and God himself never flatters. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html

**v. 24**
- **Ironside:** this is the young man who thinks he is entitled to his parents' goods and claims he has done nothing wrong. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/proverbs-28.html
- Kingcomments: he is grabbing his inheritance early. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html
- **NET:** "companion" means he is no different from a destructive criminal; TEV renders it "no better than a common thief." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki

**v. 25**
- **NET:** "greedy" is literally "wide of soul," meaning huge appetites. "Prosper" is literally "be made fat," a picture of health and plenty. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki
- Kingcomments: trusting the Lord cancels greed, because God meets every need. That is the real prosperity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html

**v. 26**
- Kingcomments: this verse rules out advice like "simply follow your heart." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html
- **NET:** "be safe" means escaping trouble. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki

**v. 27**
- **NET:** the generous person will not miss what he gave away. The verse doesn't say who curses the stingy man, but most naturally it is the poor he ignored. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki
- Kingcomments: God provides for the giver, and the poor pray for him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html

**v. 28**
- **Traditional:** a society can live for a while on a righteous generation's legacy, but when the wicked rule, freedom shrinks and people hide. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-28/
- Kingcomments: the rule of the wicked is limited, and the verse will be completely fulfilled in Christ's kingdom of peace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/proverbs-28.html
- **NET:** "rise" means coming to power, as in government. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=28&theme=wiki
